The Diademed sifaka (Propithecus diadema) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its status as a large-bodied, slow-reproducing primate endemic to the rainforests of eastern Madagascar. Neonates emerge after a gestation period of 157 days [tg = 157 days] when maternal body temperature is maintained at approximately 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a duration that aligns with values documented among other indriids. At birth, newborns have a wet weight of approximately 145 grams [Wwb = approximately 145 grams], a relatively modest mass given the species' ultimate body size, suggesting a strategy that prioritizes rapid early development under the protective cover of intense maternal care. This initial investment in offspring mass is followed by a prolonged period of dependency, during which the suckling juvenile relies entirely on milk. The transition to nutritional independence is not rapid; field data indicate that weaning occurs at 277 days after birth [tx = 277 days after birth], again under the same stable thermal regime of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], marking the end of the exclusive lactation phase.

As juveniles transition into the sub-adult stage, the pace of somatic growth accelerates, ultimately leading to the attainment of adult dimensions. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown individual is approximately 5550 grams [Wwi = approximately 5550 grams], a figure that places Propithecus diadema among the larger members of its genus. Corresponding to this robust body mass, the ultimate body length measures roughly 50 centimeters [Li = roughly 50 centimeters], with reported field measurements typically ranging between 45 and 55 centimeters (45-55 centimeters) [Li = 45-55 centimeters]. This considerable size is associated with a relatively slow life history; the maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is 21 years [am = 21 years], a figure measured when the animals are active at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. Such longevity is characteristic of primates that experience low extrinsic mortality and invest heavily in offspring survival over a protracted developmental period.

Under the typical thermal conditions of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], reproductive maturation in the Diademed sifaka occurs after an extended juvenile phase. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is reached at 1186 days after birth [tp = 1186 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. Male sifakas may achieve this milestone slightly earlier, with some field observations suggesting an age of approximately 913 days after birth [tp = 913 days after birth]. This protracted period to sexual maturity is consistent with the species' strategy of delayed reproduction, which allows for the development of complex social bonds and the acquisition of foraging skills necessary for survival in a challenging, seasonal environment. Following the onset of puberty, individuals typically do not breed immediately; a further period of social integration and territory establishment often precedes the first successful reproductive event.

Females exhibit a remarkably low reproductive rate, consistent with the species' adherence to a slow life-history pace. At a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], females produce a single infant per litter [N_R_i = single infant per litter], a standard litter size for indriids, and typically raise one litter every two years, corresponding to approximately half a litter per year [F_R_i = approximately half a litter per year]. This exceptionally low annual reproductive output is among the lowest recorded for any primate of comparable body size and reflects the energetic demands of gestating and nursing a relatively large infant over an extended period. The combination of a singleton birth and a multi-year interbirth interval means that a female may produce fewer than ten offspring over her entire reproductive lifespan, a figure that underscores the high degree of parental investment per offspring and the critical importance of infant survival to population persistence.

The transition from neonatal dependence to full nutritional independence is a gradual process that profoundly shapes the species' life history. The weaning age of 277 days after birth [tx = 277 days after birth] marks a critical nutritional transition, after which the weaned juvenile begins to incorporate solid foods, though it remains in close association with its mother for several additional years, learning to navigate the complex matrix of arboreal food resources at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The wet weight at weaning, recorded at 1350 grams [Wwx = 1350 grams], represents a near-tenfold increase over birth mass and indicates that by this stage the young sifaka has achieved approximately one-quarter of its ultimate adult mass (5550 grams) [Wwi = 5550 grams]. This substantial pre-weaning growth is supported by the mother's sustained lactation effort, after which the juvenile must rely on its own foraging proficiency. The protracted period of maternal care and the slow pace of development are key adaptations that enable Propithecus diadema to thrive as a folivorous-frugivorous specialist in the unpredictable, cyclical environment of the eastern Malagasy rainforest.
